figures.caption: Figure 1. Attack success rate by carrier × defense across three current production models (n = 14,400). The cell of primary interest is T3 under the main-matrix classifier ensemble (94.3%), compared to 0% for the same payload text in plain form (T0). T2 and T1b-abl show that neither steganographic encoding alone nor fragmented presentation alone is sufficient.

Figure 2. A T3 sample end-to-end, objective 3 (fabricated metadata). Top: the raw upstream input, ∼29 KB of JSON with two 1,044-value float arrays. No English text, no imperatives. TF-IDF and roberta-base both score this below 0.23 against a 0.5 threshold. Bottom: the ∼2 KB reconstructed report the model receives. The pipeline reverses the jitter (nearest-neighbour decode step), unshuffles, un-XORs, and renders the bytes as an xxd-style hex dump inside the analysis report. The model treats the dump as telemetry and propagates the injected [GRADE: PPB CRITICAL FAIL] field into its summary.

Figure 4. IFS trajectories at n = 964. Left: real Sierpinski (ACF 0.493). Centre-left: naive T3 with visible banding from characterfrequency bias. Centre-right: whitened intermediate (ACF 0.504, matches a real attractor). Right: final stored T3 after whitening, shuffling, and jitter for one illustrative payload (lag-1 ACF 0.035). Table 8 reports the aggregate mean lag-1 ACF after countermeasures across the broader statistical sweep (0.002). The shuffle reduces the original contraction-map autocorrelation under the first-order feature set of §4.2 and simultaneously makes semantic validation detect the current encoding.

Figure 3. Per-scan detection rate for TF-IDF and roberta-base fine-tuned on identical training data. The two agree on every cell: 100% where textual signal exists, 0% on T3. Under the dual-scan posture (flag if either fires), T1b-abl is caught via the raw-input scan alone; T3 is caught by neither.
